area.name: Car basics
area.blurb: Everyday car checks and roadside fixes, plus the science that makes them work.
area.intro: These guides cover the checks and small fixes that keep a car safe and running: oil, tires, fluids, wipers, warning lights, a flat tire, and a dead battery. Each one also explains the science under the hood, from gas laws to levers to the chemistry of antifreeze. For anything specific to your car, your owner's manual is always the final word.

guides.name: Check Your Engine Oil
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 8, help from about 10, do it alone from about 13 with an adult nearby the first few times.
guides.intro: Engine oil keeps the moving metal parts inside your engine from grinding against each other. Checking it takes a few minutes and a clean rag. Too little oil can cause major engine damage, so this is a good habit to learn early.
need: Your car's owner's manual
A clean rag or paper towel
The motor oil your car needs, if you have to add some (look on the oil fill cap or in the owner's manual)
A funnel
before: Park on level ground so the reading is accurate.
Turn the engine off. Checking with a cold engine keeps your hands away from hot parts.
Keep your hands off the radiator hose and other engine parts, which can be hot after driving.

steps.how: Park on level ground and turn off the engine. Check before you start the car, or wait 5 to 10 minutes after shutting it off so the oil can drain back down.
Open the hood and prop it the way your owner's manual shows. The manual also shows where the oil dipstick is.
Pull the dipstick all the way out. Wipe the end clean with a clean rag.
Push the dipstick all the way back in. Then pull it straight out again.
Look at where the oil film stops. It should be between the lower and upper marks.

If the oil is at or below the lower mark, add the oil your manual lists through the oil fill cap, a little at a time. On most cars, about one quart raises the level from the lower mark to the upper mark.
Give the oil a couple of minutes to settle, then wipe and dip again. Stop at the upper mark. Too much oil can be as harmful as too little.
Push the dipstick fully back in, tighten the oil fill cap, and close the hood.

pro: If you have to add oil often, have a repair shop check the car.
If the red oil pressure warning light comes on, see the dashboard warning lights guide and have the car checked.

how_it_works.subject: Physics
how_it_works.title: Why engines need a slippery film
body: When two surfaces rub, friction pushes back against the motion. Inside an engine, metal parts slide and spin past each other the whole time it runs. Motor oil spreads a thin protective layer between them so they don't scrape and collide. It also helps keep the engine from overheating.
Viscosity means how much a liquid resists flowing. Honey has high viscosity. Water has low viscosity. Oil gets thicker when it's cold and thinner when it's hot.

A label like “5W-30” gives two ratings. The number before the W is the cold-weather rating: a lower number means the oil flows more easily when the engine is cold. The number after the dash tells how thick the oil is once the engine is warmed up. Thinner oil flows easily but makes a thinner protective film, so your engine is designed for one grade. Use the one on the oil fill cap or in your owner's manual.
how_it_works.formula: friction force = μ × N (μ is how “grippy” two surfaces are; N is how hard they press together)
how_it_works.try: Put a spoonful of honey from the fridge on one plate and a spoonful of room-temperature honey on another. Tilt both plates the same amount and watch them race. The cold honey has higher viscosity, so it creeps slower, just like cold engine oil.

teach: Let your child pull and wipe the dipstick while you watch.
Ask them to read the level out loud: below the low mark, between the marks, or at full.
Show them where the oil grade is printed on the cap or in the manual.
Pair the check with a regular errand, like getting gas, so it becomes a habit.
tips: Look for the recommended oil grade on the oil fill cap. If it isn't there, check the owner's manual.
Wipe around the dipstick and oil cap before opening so dirt doesn't fall in.
Use a clean cloth on the dipstick. Grit on it can get into the engine.
Keep a quart of the right oil at home so you can top off when you need to.

mistakes.problem: Reading the dipstick on the first pull
mistakes.fix: Wipe it, push it all the way back in, and read the second pull.

mistakes.problem: Checking on a hill or slope
mistakes.fix: Park on level ground so the oil sits evenly in the engine.

mistakes.problem: Overfilling
mistakes.fix: Add a little at a time and recheck. Stop at the upper mark.

mistakes.problem: Using whatever oil is on the shelf
mistakes.fix: Use only the type your owner's manual lists.

safety: Check with the engine off.
Keep your hands away from hot engine parts like the radiator hose.
Wash your hands with soap and warm water after touching used oil.

guides.name: Check Tire Pressure and Tread
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 7, help from about 9, do it alone from about 12.
guides.intro: Tires are the only part of the car that touches the road. Keeping them at the right pressure and replacing them before the tread wears out helps the car grip, stop, and save fuel. All you need is a gauge and a penny.
need: A tire pressure gauge (keep one in the car)
A penny
Your car's tire pressure label or owner's manual
An air pump (many gas stations have one)
before: Check tires cold: the car should not have been driven for at least three hours.

steps.how: Look for the tire label on the edge of the driver's door or on the door post, or check the owner's manual. Use that number, not the one on the tire's sidewall. The sidewall number is the tire's maximum, not what your car needs.

steps.t: Make sure the tires are cold
steps.how: Check before you drive, or after the car has sat at least three hours. Warm tires read higher than cold ones.
Unscrew the valve cap, press the gauge firmly onto the valve stem, and read the psi. Write down each tire's number.
If a tire is low, add air and check again. If it's too high, press the pin in the valve stem with the edge of the gauge to let a little air out, then recheck. Screw the valve caps back on.
If your car has a spare tire, check it too.
Put a penny into a tread groove with Lincoln's head upside down and facing you. If you can see the top of his head, the tread is worn out and it's time for new tires.

steps.t: Look for wear bars and damage
steps.how: Raised bars run across the bottom of the tread grooves. If the tread is worn down level with them, replace the tires. Also look for cuts, cracks, or bulges.
Check all your tires at least once a month and before long trips.

pro: Stop using a tire that has cuts, cracks, or bulges, and have a tire shop look at it.
If the tire pressure light flashes for about a minute and then stays on, the monitoring system itself has a problem. Have a dealer or shop inspect it.

how_it_works.subject: Physics
how_it_works.title: Why cold mornings lower tire pressure
body: The air in a tire is made of tiny molecules zooming around. Every time they hit the inside of the tire, they push on it. All those pushes add up to the pressure your gauge reads.

When air warms up, the molecules move faster and hit the walls more, so pressure goes up. When air cools, they slow down and pressure drops. This is Gay-Lussac's law: if the space stays the same size, pressure rises and falls with temperature.

For car tires, AAA says pressure changes about 1 psi for every 10 °F change in temperature. So a 30-degree cold snap overnight can leave a tire about 3 psi low. That's why you check tires cold, before driving warms them up.
Low tires waste fuel, too. FuelEconomy.gov says gas mileage drops about 0.2% for every 1 psi drop in the average pressure of all four tires.
how_it_works.formula: P₁ ÷ T₁ = P₂ ÷ T₂ (P is the total gas pressure and T is temperature measured up from absolute zero)
how_it_works.try: Blow up a balloon, tie it, and measure around its middle with a string. Put it in the freezer for 30 minutes and measure again. The cold air inside pushes less, so the balloon shrinks. Let it warm up and watch it grow back.

teach: Let your child read the gauge and write the four numbers on a card.
Make the penny test a game: is Lincoln's head hidden or showing?
Have them find the door label and compare it with the sidewall so they see why the numbers differ.
Measure on a cold morning and again after a drive, just to compare. Only adjust air when the tires are cold.
tips: The tire pressure warning light is a backup, not a replacement for monthly checks. It comes on only when a tire is well below the right pressure.
Tires can lose air suddenly after hitting a pothole or curb, so check them after a hard bump.
Front and rear tires may need different pressures. The label tells you.

Tires age even when the tread looks fine. Some carmakers and tire makers recommend replacing tires that are 6 to 10 years old. The last four digits of the DOT code on the sidewall show the week and year the tire was made.

mistakes.problem: Filling to the number on the tire's sidewall
mistakes.fix: Use the pressure on the door label or in the owner's manual. The sidewall shows the maximum.

mistakes.problem: Checking right after a drive
mistakes.fix: Warm tires read high. Check when the car has sat at least three hours.

mistakes.problem: Trusting your eyes
mistakes.fix: A low tire often looks normal. Use a gauge.

mistakes.problem: Forgetting the spare
mistakes.fix: Check it each month along with the others.

safety: Replace tires when the tread is worn down to 2/32 of an inch.
Don't drive on tires with cuts, cracks, or bulges.
Keep tires at the pressure your car's maker lists.

guides.name: Change a Flat Tire
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 8, help from about 12 by handing tools and loosening lug nuts, and do it alone around the time they're learning to drive.
guides.intro: A flat tire can happen to anyone. If you're somewhere safe, you can put on the spare with the tools that came with your car. Practice once in your driveway so you're not learning on the side of the road.
need: Spare tire
The jack and lug wrench that came with your car
Owner's manual
Wheel wedges, if you have them
Tire pressure gauge
Gloves and a flashlight
before: Get to a safe spot, like a parking lot, side street, or wide shoulder, on solid, level ground away from traffic.
Turn on your hazard lights.
Put the car in Park, set the parking brake, and turn off the engine.
Get everyone out of the car and away from traffic. No one should stay inside a car that's being jacked up.
If changing the tire would put you or your passengers at risk, don't do it. Call roadside assistance instead.

steps.how: Put wheel wedges (or heavy objects) against the tire diagonally across from the flat so the car can't roll.
Take out the spare, jack, and lug wrench. Pry off the hubcap or wheel cover if there is one.
While the tire is still on the ground, turn each lug nut counterclockwise about a quarter to a half turn. Don't take them off yet.
Set the jack at the lifting point your owner's manual shows, on the car's metal frame near the flat. Plastic parts can crack if you jack on them.
Raise the car just until the flat tire is off the ground. Your manual may say how high. Never put any part of your body under the car while it's on the jack.
Remove the lug nuts by hand and put them where they won't roll away. Pull the tire straight toward you with both hands, smoothly, and lay it flat.
Line up the holes with the wheel studs and push the spare on. Make sure no mud or gravel keeps it from sitting flat against the hub. Thread the lug nuts on by hand.

steps.t: Lower and tighten in a star
steps.how: Lower the car until the spare touches the ground. Tighten the lug nuts with the wrench in a star (crisscross) pattern, not around the circle.

steps.t: Lower all the way and tighten again
steps.how: Lower the car fully, remove the jack, and go around the star pattern once more until every nut is tight.

steps.t: Check the spare and drive gently
steps.how: Check the spare's pressure; compact spares often need a higher pressure, such as 60 psi, so use the number on the spare's sidewall or in your manual. Stay within the spare's speed limit (often 50 mph) and get your regular tire fixed or replaced soon.

pro: If you're on a busy highway or don't feel safe, stay away from traffic and call roadside assistance.
Lug nuts need to be tightened to a set amount listed in your manual. If you don't have a torque wrench, have a tire shop check them as soon as possible.
If a wheel stud or lug nut looks damaged, have a shop fix it. Damaged studs may not hold the wheel on.

how_it_works.subject: Physics
how_it_works.title: Levers, torque, and the jack
body: A lug wrench is a lever. Torque is the turning force you create, and it equals how hard you push times how far your hand is from the nut. Push with 50 pounds at the end of a 1-foot handle and you make 50 pound-feet of torque. Push the same 50 pounds on a 2-foot handle and you make 100 pound-feet.

That's why you push near the end of the handle. It's also why you loosen the nuts while the tire is still on the ground. If the wheel were in the air, it would just spin. On the ground, the tire's grip on the road holds it still, so your torque goes into the nut.

A car jack trades distance for force. You crank the handle around many times, moving your hand a long way, and the car rises only a little. If you ignore friction, the work you put in equals the work you get out, so a small push over a long distance can lift a heavy load a short distance. This is called mechanical advantage.
how_it_works.formula: torque = force × lever arm; load force × distance lifted = effort force × distance moved (ignoring friction)
how_it_works.try: Open a heavy door by pushing right next to the hinges. Then push near the handle. The handle side is much easier because the lever arm is longer, so the same push makes more torque.

teach: Practice in the driveway on a nice day, with an adult handling the jack.
Let your child loosen and tighten lug nuts while the car is on the ground.
Have them draw the star pattern for your car's number of lug nuts before you start.
Find the jack points together, first in the manual and then on the car.
tips: Check your spare's pressure when you check your other tires.
Lefty-loosey: turn lug nuts counterclockwise to loosen them.
Keep gloves and a flashlight with your spare.
A temporary spare isn't made to last. Get your regular tire fixed or replaced soon.
With practice, the whole job takes about 20 minutes.

mistakes.problem: Jacking up the car before loosening the lug nuts
mistakes.fix: Loosen them a quarter to half turn while the tire is on the ground.

mistakes.problem: Putting the jack under a plastic panel
mistakes.fix: Use the jack point shown in your manual, on the metal frame.

mistakes.problem: Tightening the nuts in a circle
mistakes.fix: Use a star pattern so the wheel sits evenly against the hub.

mistakes.problem: Driving fast or far on a compact spare
mistakes.fix: Follow the speed and distance limits on the spare or in your manual.

safety: Never put any part of your body under a car held up only by a jack.
Use only the jack that came with your car, at the jack points in the manual.
Block the wheel diagonally opposite the flat.
Keep everyone out of the car and away from traffic while you work.

guides.name: Jump-Start a Car
guides.time: about 15 minutes, plus a 20 to 30 minute drive
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 10, help from about 13 by reading the manual and naming each clamp spot, and do it alone around the time they start driving.
guides.intro: When a car's battery runs down, another car's battery can help it start. Jumper cables go on in a set order that keeps sparks away from the battery. Learn the order once and you can help yourself or a neighbor.
need: Heavy-duty jumper cables (AAA suggests a six-gauge, 16-foot set)
A working car with a 12-volt battery
Both cars' owner's manuals
Safety glasses
before: Read the jump-starting section of both owner's manuals. Some cars, including some hybrids and electric cars, have special rules or shouldn't be used to jump another car.
Check that both cars use 12-volt systems.
Look at the dead battery. Don't jump it if it's cracked, bulging, leaking, smells like rotten eggs, or is frozen.
Put on safety glasses and take off rings, watches, and other metal jewelry.
Park the cars close but not touching, both in Park with the parking brakes set and the engines off.

steps.how: Turn off the headlights, radio, and other electrical items in both cars.
Attach a red clamp to the positive (+) terminal of the dead battery.
Attach the other red clamp to the positive (+) terminal of the good battery.
Attach a black clamp to the negative (−) terminal of the good battery.

Attach the last black clamp to a solid, unpainted metal part of the dead car's engine, away from the battery, such as a thick bolt. Keep the cables clear of belts and fans, and never let the clamps touch each other.
Start the working car and let it run for three to five minutes.
Start the car with the dead battery. If it cranks slowly, wait about five more minutes and try again. If it won't start after a third try, the battery probably needs replacing.

Leave both cars running and connected for three to five minutes. Then remove the clamps in reverse order: black from the bare metal, black from the good battery, red from the good battery, and red from the car you just started.
Drive for 20 to 30 minutes so the car can recharge its battery. Have the battery tested soon, especially if it's more than three years old.

pro: If the battery is cracked, bulging, leaking, or frozen, don't jump it. It needs to be replaced.
If you're unsure about any step, get a trained technician or a tow service to help.
If you hear a sharp, repeated clicking but the engine doesn't crank, the problem may be something other than the battery. Have a shop check it.
If the battery keeps going dead or you don't know why it died, have the car checked.

how_it_works.subject: Physics
how_it_works.title: Why a weak battery can't crank the engine
body: A car battery is really six small batteries, called cells, connected in a row. Each lead-acid cell makes about 2 volts, so six of them add up to 12 volts. Inside, plates of lead and lead dioxide sit in sulfuric acid, and a chemical reaction pushes electrons through any circuit you connect.
Voltage is the push. Current is how much electricity flows. The starter motor that cranks the engine needs a very high current. In a circuit, current equals voltage divided by resistance.

Every battery also has some resistance inside it, and that inside resistance tends to rise as the battery runs down or ages. With a light load, a weak battery can seem fine. Under a heavy load like the starter, its voltage drops a lot, so the starter can't get enough current to turn the engine.

Jumper cables connect the good car's battery to the dead one so they share the work. Once the good car is running, its alternator helps charge the dead battery. After your car starts, its own charging system tops the battery back up while you drive.
how_it_works.try: Look inside a flashlight that takes two or more batteries. They sit end to end, like the six cells in a car battery. Read the voltage printed on each battery and add them up to get the flashlight's total voltage.

teach: Have your child read the jump-start page of the owner's manual out loud.
Point out the + and − marks on the battery and the red and black cable colors.
With the cables not attached to anything, have them say where each clamp goes, in order: red-dead, red-good, black-good, black-metal.
Show them a good unpainted metal spot on your engine, away from the battery.
tips: Keep jumper cables in your trunk.
Running the good car's engine a little above idle can speed up charging.
On the drive afterward, keep the air conditioner and rear defroster off so more power goes to recharging.
A short drive won't fix an old battery. Have it tested.

mistakes.problem: Putting the last black clamp on the dead battery's negative terminal
mistakes.fix: Clamp it to bare metal on the engine, away from the battery, so any spark happens away from battery gases.

mistakes.problem: Letting the clamps touch each other
mistakes.fix: Hold the clamps apart and connect them one at a time.

mistakes.problem: Leaning over the battery while connecting
mistakes.fix: Stand to the side and keep your face back.

mistakes.problem: Jumping a damaged or frozen battery
mistakes.fix: Don't. Replace it.

safety: Batteries can give off hydrogen gas, which can explode. Keep sparks and flames away from the battery.
Wear safety glasses. Car batteries contain sulfuric acid, which is corrosive.
Use only a 12-volt source to jump a 12-volt car.
Keep hands, hair, and cables away from belts and fans once an engine is running.

guides.name: Check Coolant, Brake Fluid, and Washer Fluid
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 8, help from about 10, do it alone from about 13.
guides.intro: Besides oil, your car needs a few other fluids: coolant so the engine doesn't overheat or freeze, brake fluid so the brakes work, and washer fluid so you can see. Most sit in see-through tanks with marks on the side, so a quick look tells you if one is low.
need: Owner's manual (it shows where each tank is and which fluids to use)
The exact coolant and brake fluid your manual lists, if you need to add any
Windshield washer fluid
A clean rag
A funnel
before: Park on level ground with the engine off and cold.
Never open the radiator cap when the engine is hot. Hot coolant and steam can spray out under pressure.
Keep coolant and washer fluid in their original containers with the caps closed tightly, out of sight and reach of children and pets.

steps.how: Open the hood and use your owner's manual to find the coolant reservoir, brake fluid reservoir, and washer fluid tank. The coolant reservoir is a see-through plastic tank, often near the radiator. The brake fluid reservoir usually sits toward the back of the engine area on the driver's side.
Look at the side of the coolant reservoir without opening it. The level should be between the low and full marks. On some tanks, the marks are labeled hot and cold.
If it's below the low mark, add the coolant your manual lists to the reservoir, up to the mark but not higher. Leave the radiator cap alone.
Wipe around the brake fluid cap so dirt can't fall in. The level should be between the MIN and MAX marks on the side of the reservoir.
Brake fluid drops a little as the brakes wear. If it's near or below the low mark, have a shop inspect the brakes soon. Use only the brake fluid your manual lists, and never mix types.
Open the washer fluid cap and fill the tank to the top. Where temperatures drop below freezing, use a winter washer fluid that resists freezing.
Wipe up any drips right away, tighten every cap, and close the hood.
If you find yourself adding coolant or brake fluid often, have a shop look for a leak.

pro: If the brake fluid is near or below the low mark, have a shop inspect the brakes for wear or leaks as soon as possible.
If you need to add coolant often, have the cooling system checked.
If the engine is overheating or steaming, don't open the radiator cap. Let it cool and get help.

how_it_works.subject: Chemistry
how_it_works.title: How antifreeze works in winter and summer
body: Plain water freezes at 32 °F and boils at 212 °F, and both are a problem in an engine. Water that freezes in a cold engine can crack it. Water that boils turns to steam and stops cooling.

Coolant is a mix of water and antifreeze, which usually contains ethylene glycol. When something is dissolved in water, its particles make it harder for water molecules to line up into ice, so the mix freezes at a lower temperature. They also make it harder for water to escape as vapor, so the mix boils at a higher temperature. Chemists call these colligative properties: they depend on how many particles are dissolved, not on what kind they are.

More antifreeze gives more protection, up to a point. One Kia owner's manual says a half-and-half mix protects down to about −31 °F, and it warns against using more than 60% or less than 35% antifreeze. Your manual lists the right coolant for your car.
Brake fluid has its own chemistry problem. It slowly soaks up moisture from the air, and that lowers its boiling point. That's one reason to keep the cap closed and use fluid from a sealed bottle.
how_it_works.formula: drop in freezing point = K_f × m (K_f is a set number for water; m is how much is dissolved)
how_it_works.try: Fill two paper cups with the same amount of water. Stir a few spoonfuls of table salt into one. Put both in the freezer and check every 30 minutes. The plain water freezes first, while the salty water stays slushy longer because the dissolved salt lowers its freezing point. Never experiment with real antifreeze; it's poisonous.

teach: Have your child find each tank using the pictures in the owner's manual.
Ask them to read each level out loud: below, between, or above the marks.
Talk about why the radiator cap stays closed when the engine is hot.
Do the salt-water freezer test together before your first winter check.
tips: One Kia manual says to check coolant and its freeze protection at least once a year, at the start of winter, and before a trip somewhere colder. Check what your manual says.
Clean around caps before you open them so dirt doesn't get in.
Don't let brake fluid touch the car's paint. It can damage it.
Don't overfill. Too much fluid can be as harmful as too little.

mistakes.problem: Opening the radiator cap on a hot engine
mistakes.fix: Read the see-through reservoir instead, and only when the engine is cold.

mistakes.problem: Using the wrong coolant or brake fluid
mistakes.fix: Use only the type your manual lists, and don't mix types.

mistakes.problem: Using summer washer fluid in freezing weather
mistakes.fix: Switch to a winter washer fluid that resists freezing.

mistakes.problem: Storing fluids in drink bottles
mistakes.fix: Keep them in their original containers. People sometimes drink these fluids by mistake.

safety: Never open the radiator cap while the engine is hot.
Antifreeze and washer fluid are both poisonous. Antifreeze tastes sweet, which can attract children and animals.
Wipe up coolant spills and leaks right away.
Keep caps tightly closed and store bottles out of sight and reach.

guides.name: Replace Windshield Wiper Blades
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 7, help from about 9, do it alone from about 12.
guides.intro: Wiper blades are strips of rubber that clear rain and snow so you can see. Sun, weather, and use wear the rubber out, and then it streaks or skips. New blades usually click on in a few minutes.
need: New wiper blades in the right size
A towel
A tape measure
before: Turn the car off. Some cars need the wipers moved to a “service position” first; your owner's manual explains how.
Lay a towel on the windshield in case the wiper arm snaps back.

steps.how: Check your owner's manual or measure each old blade before you shop.
Lay a folded towel on the windshield under the wiper arm.
Gently lift the wiper arm up and away from the windshield.
Find the tab, button, or clip where the blade meets the arm. Press or lift it, then slide the blade down and off the hook.
Slide the new blade onto the hook until it clicks. Close any clip or latch.
Pull gently on the blade to make sure it's firmly attached.
Set the arm back down slowly. Don't let it snap onto the glass; that can crack or chip the windshield.
Replace the other blade the same way. If you used the service position, turn the car on to bring the wipers back. Spray washer fluid to test them instead of running them on dry glass.

pro: If new blades still skip or don't touch the glass evenly, the wiper frame or arm may be bent. Have a shop check it.

how_it_works.subject: Physics
how_it_works.title: Why old wipers streak
body: A wiper works like a squeegee. Its rubber edge presses against the glass and pushes water off as it slides. The friction between rubber and glass depends on how hard they press together and on the two surfaces.

New rubber has a sharp, square edge that bends to fit the curve of the windshield. Over time, the sun's ultraviolet rays, ozone, very hot and cold weather, and grit wear the rubber down. The edge gets rounded, and the rubber dries out, hardens, and cracks.

A rounded or cracked edge can't press evenly on the glass, so water slips past and leaves streaks. Also, the grip needed to start something sliding is usually a bit bigger than the grip while it slides. A stiff blade that isn't gliding smoothly may stick and then jump, which you see as skipping or hear as chattering.
how_it_works.formula: friction force = μ × N (μ depends on the two surfaces; N is how hard they press together)
how_it_works.try: Wet a bathroom mirror and pull a clean rubber spatula across it. Then press harder on one end so the edge doesn't touch evenly. Where the edge lifts, a stripe of water stays behind, just like a worn wiper leaves a streak.

teach: Let your child measure the old blades and write down the sizes.
Have them hold the towel and lift the arm while you watch.
Run a finger along an old blade and a new one to feel the difference in the edge.
Talk about why seeing clearly in rain and snow matters for safe driving.
tips: Check your blades about every six months. Many mechanics and blade makers suggest replacing them every six months to a year.
Wipe the rubber edge with a damp paper towel to remove dirt and oil.
Clear ice with a scraper or the defroster, not the wipers.
Keep gasoline, paint thinner, and other solvents away from the blades.

mistakes.problem: Letting the bare wiper arm snap onto the windshield
mistakes.fix: Keep a towel on the glass and lower the arm gently.

mistakes.problem: Buying the wrong size
mistakes.fix: Check the manual or measure each old blade before you shop.

mistakes.problem: Running wipers on dry or icy glass
mistakes.fix: Spray washer fluid first, and clear ice with a scraper or the defroster.

mistakes.problem: Not clicking the blade all the way in
mistakes.fix: Tug gently to make sure it's locked before you lower the arm.

safety: Lower the wiper arm gently. If it snaps back, it can crack or chip the glass.
Replace blades once they streak or skip. Worn blades make it harder to see in rain, snow, and dust.

guides.name: Read Dashboard Warning Lights
guides.teach_age: Learn the colors from about 8, quiz each other from about 10, and know the main lights well before driving lessons.
guides.intro: Warning lights are your car's way of telling you something needs attention. The color tells you how urgent it is, and the symbol tells you which system has a problem. Knowing the main ones helps you decide whether to keep going, pull over, or get help.
need: Your car's owner's manual (the warning light section)
A few minutes in the parked car

steps.how: Find the warning light section in your owner's manual. Symbols and meanings vary by car, so your manual is the final word.
Red means a problem that needs attention right away. Yellow or amber means something needs checking soon.
Turn the ignition to ON without starting the engine. Several warning lights glow, which shows they work. Lights like oil pressure and check engine should go out once the engine starts.

A steady light means the car's computer found a possible problem, often with emissions. Make sure the gas cap is tight; if the light stays on, have the car checked. If it flashes, the problem could cause serious damage, so avoid driving until it's repaired.
Oil pressure is low. Pull over as soon as it's safe, turn off the engine, and check the oil level. If the light stays on after adding oil, don't keep driving; have the car inspected.
The engine is overheating. Pull over when it's safe, turn off the engine, and let it cool before checking coolant or calling for help.
The charging system isn't working right; it could be the alternator or its belt, not only the battery. Get to a repair shop soon, before the battery runs down.
One or more tires are well below the right pressure. Check and fill them. If the light flashes for about a minute and then stays on, the monitoring system has a problem.

It comes on when the parking brake is set. If it stays on after you release the parking brake, the brake fluid may be low or the brakes may have a problem. Stop in a safe place; if you see a leak or the brakes don't feel right, don't drive. Have it towed.

pro: A flashing check engine light: avoid driving until a technician repairs it.
A brake light that stays on with the parking brake off, plus a leak or brakes that don't work right: don't drive; have the car towed.
An oil pressure light that stays on after adding oil: have the car inspected before driving on.
A charging system light: have the alternator and charging system checked soon.

how_it_works.subject: Physics
how_it_works.title: Sensors, the car's computer, and the tire light
body: Your car is full of sensors. A sensor measures something, like oil pressure, engine temperature, or how fast a wheel is turning, and turns it into an electrical signal. The car's computer keeps reading these signals. When a reading goes outside the safe range, the computer turns on a warning light.

The check engine light is part of the car's on-board diagnostics. When the computer finds a fault, it saves a trouble code, a short code made of letters and numbers that points to the problem. A mechanic plugs a scanner into the car to read it.

Tire pressure monitors work in one of two ways. Direct systems put a small battery-powered pressure sensor inside each tire that sends its reading to the car by radio. Indirect systems use the anti-lock brake sensors to compare how fast each wheel spins. A low tire is a little smaller around, so it has to spin faster to keep up. U.S. federal rules require the warning when a tire is 25% or more below the car maker's recommended pressure.
how_it_works.formula: distance per turn = π × tire diameter (a smaller tire turns more times to go the same distance)
how_it_works.try: Roll a big can and a small can across the floor for the same distance and count how many times each turns. The smaller can turns more times, just like a low tire. Measure each can's diameter and multiply by 3.14 to predict how far it rolls in one turn.

teach: Make flash cards from the symbols in your manual: red ones in one pile, yellow ones in another.
On the next drive, have your child watch the lights come on and go out during the bulb check.
Play “what would you do?” with each red light.
Show them where the warning light pages are in the manual.
tips: A loose or broken gas cap can turn on the check engine light. Tighten it; if that was the problem, the light may go off after several trips.
The tire pressure light warns only when a tire is well below the right pressure, so keep checking tires monthly.
Notice whether a light is steady or flashing. That can change what it means.
Keep the owner's manual in the glove box.

mistakes.problem: Ignoring a yellow light for months
mistakes.fix: Yellow means check soon. Look it up and get it looked at.

mistakes.problem: Driving on with a red oil pressure or temperature light
mistakes.fix: Pull over safely and turn off the engine. Driving on can badly damage the engine.

mistakes.problem: Guessing what a symbol means
mistakes.fix: Look it up in your owner's manual, since symbols vary by car.

mistakes.problem: Driving with the parking brake on
mistakes.fix: Make sure the brake light goes out before you drive.

safety: Treat red lights as urgent and pull over when it's safe.
Don't drive with the brake light on if the brakes feel wrong or fluid is leaking.
Avoid driving with a flashing check engine light.
Let an overheated engine cool before checking anything.

guides.name: Change Your Own Oil and Filter
guides.teach_age: Watch from about 10, help from about 13 with jobs that keep them out from under the car, and do it alone as an older teen after doing it together a few times.
guides.intro: Over time, engine oil gets dirty and its additives get used up, so it needs to be drained and replaced. Changing it yourself teaches you how your car works, but only do it with the car safely supported on ramps or jack stands. If you're not comfortable, a shop can do it.
need: The oil type and amount your owner's manual lists
A new oil filter that fits your car
Car ramps or jack stands (never just the jack)
Wheel chocks
A wrench or socket for the drain plug
An oil filter wrench
A drain pan, funnel, rags, and newspaper
Safety glasses and gloves
A clean, leak-proof container with a tight lid for the used oil
before: Read the oil change section of your owner's manual.
Let the engine cool. Used oil and some metal parts can be very hot.
Park on flat, solid ground. Raise the car on ramps or jack stands as your manual shows, set the parking brake, and chock the wheels.
Never get under a car held up only by a jack.

steps.t: Set up under the drain plug
steps.how: Spread newspaper and set the drain pan under the drain plug. Open the oil fill cap on top of the engine so the oil drains faster.
Loosen the plug counterclockwise with the wrench, then finish by hand. Let the old oil drain for several minutes.
Check the plug and its gasket for wear, and use a new gasket if your manual calls for one. Put the plug back in and tighten it to the torque your manual lists.
Move the pan under the filter. Loosen it with the filter wrench, let it drain a few seconds, then remove it by hand. Make sure its rubber gasket came off with it and isn't stuck to the engine.
Rub a thin layer of oil on the new filter's rubber gasket. This helps keep it from cracking or sticking.
Screw it on by hand until it's tight. Tighten it by hand, not with the wrench, unless your manual or the filter's instructions say otherwise.
Using a funnel, pour in the amount and type your manual lists. Put the fill cap back on.
Start the engine and let it run for about two minutes. Look around the drain plug and filter for drips. If you see a leak, shut the engine off and find the cause before driving.
Bring the car back down to level ground, turn it off, and wait about two minutes. Check the dipstick and add a little more oil if needed.

Pour the used oil into your clean container and close it tightly. Take the oil and the drained filter to a used oil collection site, such as a service station, quick lube shop, or auto parts store that accepts them. Write down the date and mileage.

pro: If you're unsure about any step, have a professional shop change the oil. Some carmakers recommend that.
If a leak won't stop, have a shop look at it before you drive.
If you don't have ramps or jack stands, don't go under the car. Have a shop do the job.

how_it_works.subject: Chemistry
how_it_works.title: Why oil wears out
body: Motor oil lubricates. It coats moving metal parts so they slide past each other with less friction. It also picks up dirt and the leftovers from burning fuel and carries them away from the pistons.

As you drive, more of that dirt builds up in the oil. The filter catches many of the particles, but over time the oil's additives get used up. Then the oil itself can start to break down: it reacts with oxygen (oxidizes) or thickens, and it can't protect the engine as well.

Used oil isn't garbage, though. It can be cleaned and re-refined into new motor oil that meets the same standards as oil made from crude. That's why recycling matters. Dumped oil pollutes water: California's recycling agency says one gallon of used oil can foul a million gallons of drinking water.
how_it_works.formula: next oil change = today's odometer reading + the interval in your manual (for example, 45,000 + 7,500 = 52,500 miles)
how_it_works.try: Rub your palms together quickly for ten seconds and feel the warmth from friction. Then put a drop of cooking oil or hand lotion on your palms and try again. The slippery film cuts the friction, which is what motor oil does for engine parts.

teach: Before the first time, read the manual's oil section together and find the drain plug and filter on the car.
Kids can hand tools, hold the funnel, pour new oil with help, and read the dipstick. Adults handle anything under the car.
Have your child work out the next change mileage and write it down.
Take the used oil to the recycling drop-off together.
tips: Your owner's manual lists the oil change interval for your car. Intervals vary by maker and model year.
Don't mix used oil with anything else, including water.
Many service stations and quick lube shops take used oil and filters at no charge.
Drain the old filter before you take it to be recycled.

mistakes.problem: Working under a car held up only by the jack
mistakes.fix: Use ramps or jack stands on flat, solid ground every time.

mistakes.problem: Leaving the old filter gasket stuck on the engine
mistakes.fix: Check that it came off with the old filter before you put on the new one.

mistakes.problem: Overtightening the new filter with a wrench
mistakes.fix: Tighten it by hand unless the instructions say otherwise.

mistakes.problem: Pouring used oil on the ground, in the trash, or down a drain
mistakes.fix: Take it to a used oil collection site.

safety: Never get under a car supported only by a jack.
Wear safety glasses and gloves.
Let the engine cool first; used oil and metal parts can be very hot.
Set the parking brake and chock the wheels.
